name: Juan Perón

meta.window: First two presidencies, 1946-1955. Won genuinely competitive elections (1946, 1951); erosions accumulated across the term.
meta.summary: Juan Perón won the 1946 and 1951 presidential elections in genuinely competitive contests, backed by organized labor and, from 1947, newly enfranchised women, and pursued broadly popular labor and social-welfare policies. Once in office, however, he progressively bent institutions: packing the Supreme Court, expropriating independent media such as La Prensa, jailing opposition leader Ricardo Balbin under contempt laws, and ruling under an extra-constitutional 'state of internal war' after 1951. A hybrid case in which democratic mandates coexisted with documented, incremental erosion of judicial, press, and civil-liberties safeguards.

editor_note: Anchored to his elected presidencies to test the hybrid end of the scale. The researcher deliberately did not score an opposition-party ban (the dissolved Labour Party was Peron's own ally) or rule-by-decree (he governed with a real, Peronist-dominated Congress). Editorial discipline (v1.1): dropped two over-matched 'extreme' indicators that failed the symmetry test at his magnitude -- prs-01 (independent press was reduced, not eliminated; La Nacion kept publishing) and civ-02 (executive detention under the state of internal war is already captured by civ-03; it was not Great-Terror-scale mass detention). 'Extreme' and 'condition' indicators are reserved for near-total capture.

scored_actions.note: The Peronist majority impeached and removed four of five Supreme Court justices plus the Attorney General, leaving a court tailored to the executive.

sources.title: Argentina's Abandonment of the Rule of Law and Its Aftermath
sources.publisher: Washington University Journal of Law & Policy

scored_actions.note: The 1949 constitutional reform (16 Dec 1949) removed the bar on immediate presidential re-election, enabling Peron to run again and win in 1951; annulled after 1955.

sources.title: Constitutional Change as a Means to Consolidate Power: Argentina 1949

scored_actions.note: Congress expropriated the leading independent daily La Prensa in April 1951 after a Peronist newsvendors' strike; other papers (e.g. La Nueva Provincia, 1950) were likewise seized.

sources.title: Argentina: The Burial of La Prensa (1951)

scored_actions.note: The expropriated La Prensa was handed to the Peronist labor confederation (CGT), converting a critical outlet into allied ownership; returned to its owners after 1955.

sources.title: Argentina: The Burial of La Prensa (1951)
The Fourth Enemy: Journalism and Power in the Making of Peronist Argentina

scored_actions.note: The 'ley de desacato' (contempt/insult law) was used to sanction and prosecute critics of Peron and Evita, criminalizing a broad category of political dissent.

sources.title: El sistema penal durante el primer peronismo (1946-1955)

scored_actions.note: Principal opposition (UCR) leader Ricardo Balbin had his parliamentary immunity stripped (1949), was arrested and sentenced to prison for desacato, and held until Peron's 1951 pardon.

sources.title: 12 de marzo de 1950: Ricardo Balbin es arrestado
sources.publisher: Legislatura de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires

scored_actions.note: Balbin faced roughly a dozen accumulated desacato prosecutions and over 297 days' detention without a final sentence, a selective legal campaign to sideline the leading opposition figure.

sources.title: El dia que Ricardo Balbin fue condenado a prision por desacato

scored_actions.note: Labour leader Cipriano Reyes and other detained opponents were tortured; a police detention center in Buenos Aires reportedly became a site of routine torture.
After the Sept 1951 coup attempt Peron decreed a 'state of internal war' (estado de guerra interno) that stayed in force until 1955, suspending ordinary civil-rights protections.

sources.title: Sobre antiperonismo y radicalizacion politica: el estado de guerra interno (1951-1955)

scored_actions.note: The declared 'state of internal war' was not a figure provided for in the 1949 constitution Peron had reformed, an emergency power invoked beyond its lawful basis.

sources.title: Sobre antiperonismo y radicalizacion politica: el estado de guerra interno (1951-1955)

wins: Won genuinely competitive elections in 1946 and 1951 and built a mass movement (Peronism) that has shaped Argentine politics ever since.
Enacted female suffrage (1947) and mobilized women voters through Eva Peron, expanding his electoral base for 1951.
Used the 1949 constitutional reform to lift the immediate re-election bar, securing a lawful path to a second term.
Neutralized institutional checks by packing the Supreme Court (1947) and consolidating the press into a pro-government system.
failures: Picked a ruinous fight with the Catholic Church in 1954-55, alienating a pillar of society and catalyzing his fall.
Economic overreach exhausted reserves and forced austerity by the early 1950s, eroding his worker base.
Failed to secure military loyalty; the 1955 Revolucion Libertadora overthrew him and drove him into 18 years of exile.
Deepened polarization so severely that the post-1955 regime banned Peronism outright, destabilizing Argentina for decades.
